chapter_theme: The one song at Neruvur (நெருவூர், Neruvai): the poet, lacking every virtue of the devotees who serve the guru and the Lord's servants, asks not to wander among priced women and vows never to forget the feet; the praise is a sequence of Krishna's deeds.

930.reading: The poet sets himself against the virtuous company who worship the guru, the devotees and the devotees' servants as equal to the Lord, and calls himself one without their conduct, worship, falling at the feet or weeping, without goodness, patience, skill, sense or steadiness; he asks not to stumble on the hill of priced women's breasts, wander in the forest of their hair and drown in the sea of their eyes, and vows not to forget in dream or waking the lotus feet given him at Vayali. The praise is Krishna's: the dark child who crawled with the mortar and broke the marutha trees, lifted the hill as an umbrella against the rain for the cattle, came through the trap of the underground chamber, and humbly drove Arjuna's chariot to break the hundred kings, and calls Murugan his nephew, at Neruvai among paddy and lotuses.
930.nuance: அடியவர் அடியவர் அடிமையும் ... நிகரென வழிபடு: the devotees honour even the servants of servants as the Lord, and the poet's list of what he lacks (நலமிலி பொறையிலி ... நிலையிலி) is the standard self-abuse set against them. In the praise எளிமை, the humility of Krishna as charioteer, is named as a virtue. The opening run about the snake-bearing devotees is hard to divide, and நிலவறை, the underground chamber, is my reading of an allusion I cannot place exactly.
